stem: You are the paediatric ED registrar reviewing a previously well 2-year-old boy brought in at 0200 with 6 hours of barking cough and stridor. He has audible biphasic stridor at rest, mild intercostal recession, pink mucosa, and is alert and interactive. He has been taking sips of water without difficulty. No drooling, no foreign-body history.

data_table.Examination: Audible biphasic stridor at rest; mild intercostal recession; chest otherwise clear; calm, no exhaustion
data_table.Investigations: No bloods or imaging performed; clinical assessment only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose; observe until stridor at rest settles and oral intake adequate (typically 1-2 hours)
options.rationale: Mild-to-moderate croup (intermittent stridor at rest, mild recession, alert, well perfused) is treated with a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe or life-threatening croup. Observation is tied to clinical improvement, not a fixed clock; peak dexamethasone effect is 1-2 hours. Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 flat dose plus oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg; admit to short stay for 3 hours after the dose
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline plus 0.6 mg/kg dexamethasone is reserved for severe or life-threatening croup with marked recession, agitation, exhaustion, or hypoxia; using it for mild-to-moderate disease overtreats. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Intubation in theatre by ENT and anaesthetics with transfer to the paediatric intensive care unit for ongoing respiratory support
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for impending respiratory failure with exhaustion, cyanosis, or altered consciousness, none of which are present here. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Empirical intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg and ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg with admission for paediatric sepsis workup including blood cultures
options.rationale: Bacterial tracheitis or epiglottitis would feature toxicity, drooling, and rapid progression; classic mild-to-moderate viral croup does not require antibiotics or sepsis workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium 250 micrograms; reassess respiratory work and stridor at rest 20 minutes later in resus
options.rationale: Bronchodilators have no role in upper-airway obstruction from croup; they neither relieve stridor nor address subglottic oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Croup severity is graded by stridor (none, on exertion, at rest), work of breathing, mental state, and oxygenation. Mild-to-moderate croup features stridor at rest with mild recession but no agitation, pallor, or hypoxia. RCH gives a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild-to-moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe or life-threatening disease. Nebulised adrenaline (flat 5 mL of 1:1000) is added for severe disease, with a minimum 3-hour observation after the adrenaline because effects last 30 to 60 minutes. Observation after dexamethasone alone is tied to clinical resolution rather than a fixed clock.
key_points: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose for mild-to-moderate croup per RCH
Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe or life-threatening croup
Observation after dexamethasone alone is to clinical resolution, not a fixed 4 hours
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 flat dose for severe disease, with 3-hour post-adrenaline observation
Antibiotics and bronchodilators have no role in viral croup
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone onset is 30 to 60 minutes and effect lasts 24 to 48 hours; oral, intramuscular, and nebulised routes are equivalent in efficacy.

stem: A 3-year-old girl presents to her general practitioner with 24 hours of right-sided ear pain following a recent viral upper respiratory tract infection. She is non-Aboriginal, was breastfed for 6 months, and lives with parents who do not smoke. She has been more irritable but is drinking well and ate her dinner. She has had one previous episode of otitis media 14 months ago which resolved spontaneously. On otoscopy the right tympanic membrane is red, opaque, and bulging with poor mobility; the left is normal. There is no otorrhoea.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, RR 24, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 38.1
data_table.Examination: Right TM erythematous, bulging, opaque; no perforation; no mastoid tenderness; alert and playful in waiting room

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic management decision?

options.text: Prescribe immediate oral amoxicillin 30 mg per kg twice daily for 5 days due to the bulging tympanic membrane
options.rationale: Immediate antibiotics are indicated under 6 months or in higher-risk groups; in a well low-risk child over 2 years a watchful waiting strategy is recommended even when the membrane is bulging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence a delayed prescription of oral cefalexin to be filled if symptoms worsen within the next 6 hours
options.rationale: Cefalexin has poor middle-ear penetration and is not a recommended first-line agent for otitis media; the timeframe also undercuts watchful waiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Provide analgesia with paracetamol or ibuprofen and review in 48 hours, with antibiotics if no improvement
options.rationale: Analgesia and watchful waiting for 48 hours is recommended in low-risk children over 2 years without high-risk features; antibiotics are added only if symptoms persist or worsen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer the child to an ear nose and throat surgeon for consideration of ventilation tube insertion immediately
options.rationale: Surgical referral applies to recurrent or chronic otitis media with effusion and hearing loss, not a first significant episode in 14 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media)

options.text: Prescribe oral co-trimoxazole as covers respiratory pathogens including resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.rationale: Co-trimoxazole is not first-line for otitis media in Australia and has rising resistance among pneumococcal isolates; amoxicillin is preferred when antibiotics are indicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in well children is largely self-limiting and AU antibiotic guidance favours analgesia plus watchful waiting unless high-risk features are present. Immediate antibiotics are warranted under 6 months of age, in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children at risk of chronic suppurative otitis media, with bilateral disease under 2 years, otorrhoea, or systemic toxicity. The first-line oral antibiotic when needed is amoxicillin at high dose; second-line for true type-I penicillin allergy is azithromycin. Symptom resolution at 48 to 72 hours is the trigger to add or escalate therapy.
key_points: Watchful waiting is appropriate for low-risk children over 2 years without otorrhoea or systemic features
Immediate antibiotics for under 6 months, bilateral disease under 2 years, perforation/otorrhoea, or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children at risk
Amoxicillin 30 mg/kg twice daily is first line when antibiotics are given
Analgesia is the most important short-term intervention
explanation.pearls: AMH and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic endorse 48-hour watchful waiting in low-risk children over 2 years even with a bulging tympanic membrane.

stem: A 4-year-old boy presents on day 6 of fever above 39 with persistent fever despite paracetamol. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, a strawberry tongue with cracked red lips, polymorphous truncal rash, and unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy 2 cm in diameter. He has erythematous palms with mild swelling. Streptococcal swab is negative and there is no contact with measles. Blood tests show neutrophilia, raised CRP, and thrombocytosis. He is reviewed in a paediatric inpatient unit. A baseline echocardiogram is being arranged.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 28, BP 96/58, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 39.4
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection; red cracked lips; strawberry tongue; polymorphous rash; right cervical lymphadenopathy 2 cm; erythematous swollen palms
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.4 x10^9/L (N 14.8), CRP 142 mg/L, platelets 612 x10^9/L; ASOT pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure and discharge with paracetamol; review only if fever lasts beyond day 14 of illness presentation
options.rationale: Delaying treatment beyond day 10 substantially increases coronary aneurysm risk; the priority is IVIG administration within the window. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin and oral roxithromycin for presumed group A streptococcal scarlet fever overlap
options.rationale: Scarlet fever does not produce conjunctivitis, mucositis, or palmar oedema; misdiagnosis delays IVIG and increases aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Oral aspirin 30 mg/kg/day in four divided doses without intravenous immunoglobulin and reassess at day 10
options.rationale: Aspirin alone is insufficient and does not reduce coronary aneurysm rates; IVIG is the disease-modifying treatment within the 10-day window. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg as a single infusion over 10 hours plus aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses
options.rationale: Five criteria of fever plus four of conjunctivitis, mucositis, rash, extremity changes, and cervical lymphadenopathy confirm Kawasaki disease; IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days reduces coronary aneurysm rate from 25 percent to under 5 percent, with adjunct aspirin. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse alone with paracetamol around the clock for symptomatic relief
options.rationale: Adjunctive steroids are considered in high-risk or IVIG-resistant disease, not as monotherapy first line in straightforward Kawasaki within the IVIG window. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is diagnosed by fever lasting 5 days or more with at least 4 of bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes, polymorphous rash, extremity changes, and cervical lymphadenopathy at least 1.5 cm. IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion within 10 days of fever onset cuts coronary aneurysm risk from around 25 percent to under 5 percent. High-dose aspirin is added until afebrile then reduced to antiplatelet dose. Baseline and follow-up echocardiograms are mandatory.
key_points: 5 days fever + 4 of 5 features confirms diagnosis
IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days dramatically reduces coronary aneurysm risk
Aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg/day initially then 3 to 5 mg/kg/day antiplatelet
Echocardiogram at baseline and follow-up 6 to 8 weeks
explanation.pearls: Kawasaki disease key threshold: IVIG 2 g/kg within day 10 of fever drops coronary aneurysm rate from 25 percent to under 5 percent; aspirin is adjunct, not substitute.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease
